about.length_note: About half an hour. This class covers five topics and one debate. Each idea gets a short beat and a check question, so you can stop after any question. A good place to split it in two is just before the Phoenicians.

say.text: Welcome to class 19. Today's big question: how did a few kings come to rule huge areas, and how did they keep hold of them?

show.text: Iron Age Empires: Assyria, Babylon and Persia

say.text: Last time we saw the Bronze Age world fall apart. The Near East's Iron Age is usually dated from about 1200 BCE, the same time as that collapse.

show.text: c. 1200 BCE: Bronze Age collapse and the start of the Iron Age in the Near East

say.text: First idea: iron. To make it, smiths heated iron ore with charcoal in a furnace, at around 1200 degrees Celsius.

show.text: Iron ore | Charcoal | Furnace at about 1200 °C | Usable iron

say.text: Nobody knows for sure where iron was first smelted. The very earliest iron objects may have come from meteorites.

show.text: A dark, heavy piece of meteorite iron resting on a smith's workbench

say.text: So why did iron spread? Iron ore was easier to find than the copper and tin that bronze needs.

show.text: Iron ore: easy to find

ask.q: Why did iron spread so widely?
ask.right: Iron ore was easier to find than the copper and tin needed for bronze.
wrong: Only one empire was allowed to make it.
Iron falls from the sky in large amounts.
Iron is much softer than bronze, so it is cheaper.
ask.why: Copper and tin were harder to get, while iron ore was more widely available.

say.text: You may hear that the Hittites kept iron a secret, and it spread when their kingdom fell. Scholars no longer accept that old theory.

show.text: Old story: one people guarded the secret | Now: it spread slowly, over centuries, from many hands

say.text: And it travelled far. Iron furnaces turn up in Nigeria by about 750 BCE. By about 500 BCE, smiths in China's state of Wu were making cast iron.

show.text: A world map with three marks: Anatolia and the Near East, Opi in southeast Nigeria, and the state of Wu in southern China

say.text: Second idea: what is an empire? It is one state that rules many different peoples. Today we meet three empires, and the tools they used to hold on.

show.text: Empire: one state, many peoples

say.text: Here is a first look. The Assyrian empire lasted about 325 years by one count, Babylon's only about 87, and Persia's about 220. Counts of Assyria's start differ, from about 934 to about 900 BCE.

show.text: How long each empire lasted

say.text: Assyria first. Its kings ruled from northern Iraq and built an empire stretching from western Iran toward Egypt.

show.text: A map of the Near East with the Assyrian heartland in northern Iraq and arrows toward western Iran and toward Egypt

say.text: Assyria ruled in two ways. A province had a governor sent by the king. A vassal kingdom kept its own ruler, but owed tribute and loyalty.

show.text: Province: governor sent by the king | Vassal kingdom: own ruler, pays tribute, stays loyal

ask.q: A conquered land keeps its own king, but pays tribute and owes loyalty to Assyria. What is it?
ask.why: A province had an Assyrian governor. A vassal kingdom kept its own ruler.

say.text: Under Tiglath-pileser III, who took the throne in 745 BCE, more conquered kingdoms became provinces run by governors.

show.text: 745 BCE: Tiglath-pileser III becomes king of Assyria

say.text: A third tool was moving people. Assyria deported people from rebellious lands. This was one way Mesopotamian empires kept control.

show.text: Deportation: forced movement of people

say.text: An example: in 722 BCE Assyria conquered the kingdom of Israel. It deported many people from Samaria and brought in deportees from other lands to take their place.

show.text: 722 BCE: Assyria conquers Israel and moves people in and out of Samaria

say.text: This tied distant provinces into one system. It also split up families and broke apart communities. It was hard, human suffering.

show.text: Control, and a cost in human lives

ask.q: What was one purpose of Assyrian deportation?
ask.right: It helped the king keep control of rebellious lands.
wrong: It was a reward for the most loyal towns.
It was mainly a way to find new iron mines.
It was a favour to the families who were moved.
ask.why: Deportation was a tool of control. It broke up communities and tied provinces into one system.

say.text: Assyria also had royal roads. They carried the king's letters between major cities, and they helped armies and officials move too.

show.text: A straight packed-earth road with a rider carrying a clay tablet toward a walled city

say.text: Kings also ruled through knowledge. Ashurbanipal gathered a huge library at Nineveh. He sent scholars to copy texts, especially from Babylonian temples.

show.text: 30,000+ clay tablets

say.text: Around 612 BCE Nineveh was sacked. Babylonian and Median campaigns ended the Assyrian empire in 609 BCE.

show.text: 612 BCE: Nineveh falls | 609 BCE: end of the Assyrian empire

say.text: Now Babylon. Nabopolassar took the throne of Babylon in 626 BCE and led the conquest of Assyria.

show.text: 626 BCE: Nabopolassar founds the Neo-Babylonian dynasty

say.text: His son Nebuchadnezzar II reigned from about 605 to 562 BCE. Babylon became the great imperial capital, taking Nineveh's place.

show.text: Nebuchadnezzar II, about 605 to 562 BCE

say.text: Babylon borrowed Assyria's deportation tool. Judah was a vassal of Babylon. After a failed revolt, many Judahites were exiled to Babylon in 597 BCE.

show.text: 597 BCE: first exile from Judah | 586 BCE: Judah's elite in exile in Babylon

say.text: Babylon's greatness was short. In 539 BCE the Persian king Cyrus defeated its last king, and entered Babylon without a battle.

show.text: 539 BCE: Cyrus takes Babylon

ask.q: Who ended the Babylonian empire in 539 BCE?
ask.why: Cyrus defeated Nabonidus, Babylon's last king, in 539 BCE.

say.text: Now Persia. Cyrus II, called Cyrus the Great, founded the Achaemenid Empire. He inherited his father's throne in Anshan in 559 BCE.

show.text: 559 BCE: Cyrus inherits the throne of Anshan | 539 BCE: Babylon falls

say.text: Cyrus left a clay cylinder at Babylon. It was found there in 1879 by a British Museum excavation.

show.text: A small, broken barrel of baked clay covered in rows of cuneiform writing, in a museum case

say.text: A tablet with the same text was later identified. The Assyriologist Irving Finkel thinks scribes made copies there and sent them out across the empire.

show.text: One message, many copies

say.text: The empire grew huge, so it needed organizing. That job fell to Darius I, who ruled from 522 to 486 BCE. By his own inscriptions, he most wished to be remembered as lawgiver and organizer.

show.text: Darius I, 522 to 486 BCE

say.text: He completed the division of the empire into satrapies, which are provinces. He also fixed the yearly tribute due from each one.

show.text: Satrapy = a province | Satrap = its governor | Tribute = a fixed yearly payment

ask.right: A governor of a province, appointed by the king
wrong: A road that carried the king's messages
A clay tablet with a royal decree
ask.why: Each satrapy was run by a satrap, a governor appointed by the king.

say.text: Darius worried that a governor might build his own power base. So he named a separate military commander who answered only to him.

show.text: Satrap: runs the province | Military commander: answers only to the king

ask.q: Why did Darius name a separate military commander in each province?
ask.right: So the governor could not build a power base and rebel.
wrong: So the governor would have fewer tax duties.
So the roads could be built faster.
So the commander could collect the tribute.
ask.why: Splitting power between governor and commander made rebellion harder.

say.text: Royal inspectors, the King's Eyes and Ears, also travelled the empire, checking on loyalty and efficiency.

show.text: The King's Eyes and Ears

say.text: Darius took much of this structure from the Assyrians. But his use of tribute was new. Before, it was a kind of protection money. Darius treated it as a tax.

show.text: Before: tribute as protection money | Darius: tribute as tax

say.text: He also standardized coinage, weights and measures. That made trade and tax collecting easier across the empire.

show.text: Coinage | Weights | Measures

say.text: Persia did not run everything from the centre. Local temples and villages helped with administration and tax collection. Practices differed from place to place.

show.text: Local helpers, not one uniform system

say.text: Now the road. The Royal Road ran from Susa to Sardis, about 1,677 miles.

show.text: 1,677 miles

say.text: Darius improved a road network that already existed. The western parts may first have been built by Assyrian kings.

show.text: A line from Susa in the east to Sardis in the west, with rest stations marked along it

say.text: The road carried a state relay of mounted couriers. One modern article says a message could cross the empire in as little as seven days.

show.text: A courier on a horse handing a sealed message to a fresh rider at a rest station

ask.q: What was the Royal Road mainly used for?
ask.right: Administration and military movement, such as relaying messages
ask.why: The road's primary functions were administrative and military.

say.text: Now a different kind of power: the Phoenicians. They lived on the eastern Mediterranean coast, in today's Lebanon. Their land was poor for farming, so they turned to the sea.

show.text: The eastern Mediterranean coast with the cities of Tyre, Sidon and Byblos marked

say.text: They traded timber, metals and textiles between Egypt, Mesopotamia, Anatolia and Greece. Tyre founded Carthage in North Africa around 814 BCE.

show.text: c. 814 BCE: Tyre founds Carthage

say.text: Phoenicia itself did not stay free. Assyria and then Persia conquered the homeland. After that, Carthage became an independent state.

show.text: Homeland conquered, colony independent

say.text: The Phoenicians are linked with the alphabet. It had 22 letters, all for consonants. That was much easier to learn than hundreds of hieroglyphs.

show.text: 22 letters

say.text: Greeks adopted and adapted the Phoenician alphabet in the 9th to 8th century BCE, after trading with them.

show.text: 9th to 8th century BCE: Greeks adapt the Phoenician alphabet

ask.q: What did the Phoenician alphabet's 22 letters stand for?
ask.why: It was an alphabet of 22 consonants, much simpler than hieroglyphs.

say.text: Next door lived the early Hebrew societies, the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. Both kingdoms are well attested in archaeology and in texts from their neighbours.

show.text: The Levant with the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah, and Phoenicia on the coast

say.text: A fragment found at Tel Dan in 1993 mentions a 'king of Israel' and a 'house of David'. The writing is Aramaic, from the late 9th or early 8th century BCE.

show.text: A broken stone slab with a few lines of Aramaic letters, found in the north of Israel

say.text: Their story ties to the empires you have just met. Assyria conquered Israel in 722 BCE. Babylon destroyed Judah by 586 BCE.

show.text: 722 BCE: Assyria conquers Israel | 586 BCE: Judah devastated by Babylon

say.text: After Persia took Babylon, Cyrus's edict ended the exile in 538 BCE. The Second Temple in Jerusalem was built between 520 and 515 BCE.

show.text: 538 BCE: edict of Cyrus | 520 to 515 BCE: Second Temple built

ask.q: Which empire conquered the kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE?
ask.why: Assyria conquered Israel in 722 BCE. Babylon came later and destroyed Judah.

say.text: Last idea, a debate. Much of what we know about Israel and Judah comes from the Bible, a sacred text. How should historians use a sacred text as evidence? This question is about evidence, not about faith.

show.text: Debate: religious texts as historical evidence

say.text: One approach treats the Bible as an artifact to examine. It is not taken as an unquestioned truth, and finds are not treated as mere illustrations of it.

show.text: Examine it, don't just assume it

say.text: Finkelstein and Silberman argue that key biblical narratives link to the Judean kingdom of the 7th century BCE. They still call the Bible important testimony for early Israel.

show.text: Link to the 7th century BCE kingdom of Judah | Still important testimony

say.text: Another scholar's view: the exile in Babylon pushed people to gather old traditions. Those were woven into a grand narrative with a clear historical core.

show.text: Exile: old traditions gathered together

say.text: Cross-checking helps. Before the Nineveh tablets were found, almost everything about Assyria came from the Bible and classical historians. Then the tablets let Assyrians speak in their own words.

show.text: Before: Bible and classical historians | After: thousands of Assyrian tablets

say.text: But Assyrian royal inscriptions are not neutral either. They show the king as divinely supported, defeating enemies and punishing rebels.

show.text: Kings' inscriptions have a purpose too

say.text: So a sacred text and a royal inscription get the same questions. Who wrote it, when, for whom, and why? And what do independent sources say?

show.text: Who wrote it? | When? | For whom? | Why? | What do other sources say?

ask.q: What is a good way to use a religious text as historical evidence?
ask.right: Ask who wrote it, when and why, and compare it with independent evidence.
wrong: Accept every detail as exact history.
Reject all of it because it is religious.
Use it only when archaeologists have already proved every line.
ask.why: Historians treat sacred texts like other sources: ask who wrote them and why, and compare them with outside evidence.

say.text: Same time elsewhere: Confucius was born in 551 BCE, so he was about 12 when Cyrus entered Babylon. The Buddha lived in India in these years too, though his dates are debated.

show.text: 551 BCE: Confucius born | 539 BCE: Cyrus enters Babylon | Buddha: 563 or 480 BCE birth, uncertain

say.text: Let's recap. Iron spread because ore was easy to find. Assyria used governors, vassals, deportation and roads. Babylon followed. Persia added satraps, checks, fixed tribute and the Royal Road.

show.text: Iron | Assyria | Babylon | Persia | Phoenicians and Hebrews | Weighing sacred texts

say.text: Next time we meet thinkers and teachers: the Buddha, Confucius, the Greeks and the prophets. You've just seen the world they lived in.

show.text: Next: Thinkers and Teachers

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Iron furnaces and slag are found at Opi in southeast Nigeria. Around the same time, Greeks were adopting the Phoenician alphabet (9th to 8th century BCE).
Tiglath-pileser III takes the Assyrian throne and turns more conquered lands into provinces.
Ashurbanipal rules Assyria and gathers the Nineveh library.
Nineveh is sacked, and the Assyrian empire ends soon after.
The birth of the Buddha in India; historians still debate the date.
Confucius is born in China. His contemporaries included Pythagoras, Heraclitus and Parmenides in Greece.
Cyrus takes Babylon. Confucius was about 12 years old.
Darius I rules Persia and organizes the empire.
Metalworkers in the southern Chinese state of Wu make cast iron.

other_side.claim: The Hittites kept iron-making a secret, and it spread when their kingdom fell.
other_side.other_view: This old theory is no longer accepted. Iron objects appear in the Near East for centuries before the Hittites fell, and the technology seems to have spread slowly.

other_side.claim: Darius I invented the system of twenty satrapies.
other_side.other_view: Britannica says Cyrus began the organization and Darius completed it. Herodotus lists twenty tribute districts. Modern scholars doubt this neat picture, because the number and borders of satrapies shifted over time.

other_side.claim: The Cyrus Cylinder is the first charter of human rights.
other_side.other_view: It is often called that, and exhibitions say Cyrus's tolerance has inspired many people. But since its rediscovery it has also been used to promote political agendas. Curators urge asking what Cyrus himself was thinking.

other_side.claim: The Bible's account of a great united monarchy under David and Solomon is historical.
other_side.other_view: Scholars disagree. The kingdoms of Israel and Judah are well attested. Whether a great united monarchy existed in the 10th century BCE is still debated between maximalists and minimalists. Some scholars say the evidence for an extensive early kingdom is too weak. Others say the Bible has a historical core.

other_side.claim: The Buddha lived from about 563 to 483 BCE.
other_side.other_view: This was the common dating among early 20th-century historians. Some now place his birth about 480 BCE, and the dates remain uncertain.
